pageData.title: The Caral-Supe / Norte Chico Civilization
pageData.para1: The Caral-Supe / Norte Chico Civilization. The Caral-Supe civilization - also known as the Norte Chico civilization - was a complex pre-Columbian society located in the Norte Chico region of what is now Peru, positioned to take advantage of three rivers: the Fortaleza, the Pativilca, and the Supe. Flourishing some 5,000 years ago, in the Late Archaic period of the central Andes, it has been established as the oldest known civilization in the Americas. This civilization matters because it proved that monumental urban architecture and complex social organization arose in the Americas extraordinarily early - and, unusually, without ceramics at its foundation, a society built instead on what its rivers, fields, and the nearby Pacific could provide.
pageData.para2: The city of Caral sits on a dry desert terrace overlooking the green valley of the Supe river, and features complex and monumental architecture, including six large pyramidal structures; the city's plan, its pyramids, and the elite residential group show clear evidence of ceremonial functions. Among the artifacts found at Caral is a quipu - a knotted textile piece that archaeologists believe was a method of keeping records - and a geoglyph was discovered just west of the city in 2000. Sophisticated government is assumed to have been required to manage the ancient Norte Chico, though questions remain over its organization, and notably, no evidence of warfare has been found. Its monumental scale and careful ceremonial planning continue to reveal the complexity of Caral society to archaeologists. Remarkably intact thanks to its early abandonment and late discovery, Caral was occupied only twice more, and never systematically, leaving its plazas and pyramids to sleep beneath the desert until modern archaeology woke them.

pageData.title: The Chavín Culture
pageData.para1: The Chavin Culture. The Chavin culture was a highly developed civilization of pre-Columbian Peru that flourished between about 900 and 200 BCE, its artistic influence spreading throughout the northern and central Andes. Its great religious center, Chavin de Huantar, became an important Andean pilgrimage site - though the site may not have been the actual center of origin of the culture and its style, whose roots lie in the Initial Period (about 1800-900 BCE), when a sedentary agricultural way of life became fully established; important regional manifestations of the style are found at sites such as Kotosh. The significance of Chavin is that for the first time, many of the local and regional cultures of the area were unified by a common ideology or religion - a shared spiritual horizon whose imagery, from the Paracas to the Incas, helped spread Chavin ideas across the Andes and into later empires.
pageData.para2: At the heart of the religion stood the Staff Deity, associated with agricultural fertility and usually shown holding a staff in each hand - a forerunner of the Andean creator god Viracocha - celebrated in works like the Raimondi Stela, a two-metre granite slab with the god incised in low relief, and in carvings that form a transformational series changing progressively from human to jaguar form. The temple at Chavin de Huantar, measuring a hundred metres in length, enclosed its rites in complex interiors: an important feature of the cult was a priesthood of shamans who put themselves into trances with hallucinogens. Votive offerings from distant lowland jungles confirm the far-reaching influence of the cult. The site and the culture entered into decline sometime in the 3rd century BCE, for reasons that remain unknown.

pageData.title: The Moche Culture
pageData.para1: The Moche Culture. The Moche culture was a sophisticated coastal civilization that flourished along the river valleys of northern Peru from the 1st to the 8th century CE, its influence reaching from the Piura valley south over 350 kilometers to the Nepena valley. They were intensive farmers, channeling streams from the Andes into irrigation canals to grow crops such as corn and beans, and with that agricultural wealth they supported urban centers and built impressive structures - adobe pyramids like the great Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna, terraced platforms, palaces, courtyards, and plazas. This civilization matters because its artists produced what stands as some of the finest naturalistic pottery in pre-Columbian America - mold-made vessels with their characteristic stirrup spouts, portrait heads of people, animals, and plants, and painted scenes that open a window onto Moche ceremonial and daily life.
pageData.para2: Those painted vessels show a society that was aggressive and hierarchical: scenes of the sacrifice of prisoners and ritual combat, dignitaries in splendid regalia, and fortified structures - the Moche dispersed their communities to preserve precious irrigated land. Their burial traditions matched that hierarchy: at Huaca Rajada near Sipan, archaeologists uncovered elaborate tombs filled with jewelry, their occupants' skeletal remains suggesting men significantly taller than the average Moche adult, each tomb with a compartment containing miniature representations of the dead lord's world. Gold and copper alloy masks, regalia, and masterful metalwork accompanied them. The Moche world was eventually undone in part by the very forces that sustained it - the fragile ecology of desert valleys fed by Andean streams - leaving their adobe cities and painted lords to tell the tale of their world.

pageData.title: The Nazca Culture
pageData.para1: The Nazca Culture. The Nazca culture was an ancient civilization that flourished on the southern coast of Peru between 200 BCE and 600 CE, settling the Nazca valley and its neighbors - the Pisco, Chincha, Ica, Palpa, and Acari valleys - with their principal religious and urban sites at Cahuachi and Ventilla. Cahuachi, on the south bank of the Nazca River fifty kilometers inland, was a site of pilgrimage and the Nazca religious capital, where postholes suggest canopies once protected worshippers from the sun and textile scenes link religious gatherings to harvest festivals. The culture matters above all for the Nazca Lines: great geoglyphs etched into the desert floor - geometric shapes, or animals such as the hummingbird, the spider, even a killer whale - including straight lines up to twenty kilometers long whose exact purpose remains debated, perhaps connecting sacred sites or pointing to water sources.
pageData.para2: To survive under the present threat of drought, the Nazca built an extensive network of underground aqueducts, galleries, and cisterns to ensure a good water supply during the dry months. Their pottery is polychrome, sometimes modeled in the culture's later phases, and counted amongst the finest of ancient Peru, decorated with mythical transformational creatures - especially felines - and with trophy-heads, which also appear as miniature border decorations in their textiles; the presence of highland vicuna wool in those textiles is evidence of established trade with the highland cultures. Fine pottery and textiles were buried with the dead, with no particular distinction between male and female graves. In their ceramics, their featherwork, and their vast desert drawings, the Nazca left one of the most distinctive artistic legacies of the ancient Andes.

pageData.title: The Tiwanaku & Wari Empires
pageData.para1: The Tiwanaku & Wari Empires. The Tiwanaku and Wari empires were the two great powers of the Andean Middle Horizon (600-1000 CE). Tiwanaku took its name from the ruins near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia - now a UNESCO World Heritage site - where its Kalasasaya platform and the structure known as the Palacio stand, the Kalasasaya holding the monolithic Gateway of the Sun, carved with a staff-carrying Doorway God flanked by winged figures, a god variously described as a Sun god or a thunder god. Wari, exploiting the diverse landscapes of Peru's coast and highlands as it flourished between about 450 and 1000 CE from its capital at Huari in the Peruvian highlands, constructed an empire administered by provincial capitals connected by a large road network - methods of maintaining an empire, and an artistic style, that would have a lasting influence on the Andes.
pageData.para2: Both states were gifted agriculturalists. The Wari constructed canals to irrigate terraced fields, and the economic stability this brought allowed them to resist the thirty-year drought at the end of the 6th century CE that contributed to the decline of their neighbors; at their administrative site of Pikillacta, with its strictly controlled single winding entrance, archaeologists found forty miniature greenstone figures of elite citizens. Their art centered on the Staff Deity, with plants, the San Pedro cactus flower, pumas, condors, and above all llamas - testimony to the importance of the herds. Why these empires fell is still debated: theories range from over-extension to another extended drought in the 9th century, but whatever the reasons, the region returned to a world of competing local powers until the rise of the Inca.
